title: Robotics & Agricultural Robotics
summary: Machines that sense, decide and act in the real world, with field agriculture as the hardest proving ground: uneven ground, changing light, living plants. The threshold is uncertainty: every sensor lies a little, so robots estimate their state rather than know it.
sources: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh, Scaramuzza: Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots
Bechar & Vigneault: Agricultural robots for field operations (2016)

nodes.label: Robot Kinematics
nodes.summary: Forward kinematics maps joint angles to where the tool is; inverse kinematics finds the joint angles for a target.
nodes.outcome: Compute forward kinematics for a two-link arm.
nodes.check: Why is inverse kinematics harder than forward kinematics?
nodes.answer: It may have several solutions, or none, and usually needs solving nonlinear equations.

nodes.label: Motors & Actuators
nodes.summary: DC, stepper and servo motors, gearing, and torque–speed curves.
nodes.outcome: Choose a motor and gear ratio for a wheel load.
nodes.check: Why might a robot use a stepper motor for a seed-spacing mechanism?
nodes.answer: It moves in precise, repeatable steps without needing position feedback.

nodes.label: Sensors: Encoders, IMU, Lidar, Cameras
nodes.summary: Each sensor measures something indirect, with noise, bias and failure modes.
nodes.outcome: Match sensors to measurement needs and list each one's failure modes.
nodes.check: Why does integrating a gyroscope's angular rate give a heading that drifts?
nodes.answer: Small bias and noise in the rate are integrated, so the error grows over time.

nodes.label: "GPS gives centimetre accuracy out of the box"
nodes.summary: Standard GNSS is accurate to metres; centimetre accuracy for row crops needs RTK corrections from a base station.
nodes.outcome: Explain what RTK adds to GNSS.
nodes.check: Roughly how accurate is standard consumer GPS, and what upgrades it to centimetres?
nodes.answer: A few metres; RTK (real-time kinematic) corrections from a base station bring it to about 2 cm.

nodes.label: Odometry & Dead Reckoning
nodes.summary: Estimating motion from wheel rotation; slip on soil makes the error grow without bound.
nodes.outcome: Compute odometry for a differential-drive robot and predict its drift.
nodes.check: A field robot's wheels slip in mud. What happens to its odometry estimate?
nodes.answer: It overestimates distance travelled, and the position error grows.

nodes.label: "A robot goes exactly where it is told"
nodes.summary: Commanded motion and actual motion differ (slip, backlash, load); robots must sense and correct.
nodes.outcome: Design a feedback correction for commanded motion.
nodes.check: Why does a robot told to drive 10 m straight end up off course?
nodes.answer: Wheel slip, uneven ground and motor differences make actual motion differ from commands; without feedback the errors accumulate.

nodes.label: Sensor Fusion & the Kalman Filter
nodes.summary: Combine a motion prediction with noisy measurements, each weighted by its uncertainty. Troublesome because the robot's position becomes a probability distribution.
nodes.outcome: Run one predict–update cycle of a 1D Kalman filter.
nodes.check: In a Kalman filter, when should the estimate trust the new measurement more than the prediction?
nodes.answer: When the measurement's uncertainty is smaller than the prediction's.

nodes.label: Feedback Control for Robots
nodes.summary: PID and trajectory tracking turn plans into motor commands while rejecting disturbances.
nodes.outcome: Tune a PID controller to follow a crop row.
nodes.check: A row-following robot weaves from side to side. Which PID gain is most likely too high?
nodes.answer: The proportional gain (or too little derivative damping).

nodes.label: Computer Vision
nodes.summary: Cameras plus ML for detection and segmentation: crops vs weeds, fruit ripeness, row lines.
nodes.outcome: Train and evaluate a crop–weed segmentation model.
nodes.check: Why do vision models for farms often fail when moved to a new field or season?
nodes.answer: Distribution shift: lighting, growth stage, soil and varieties differ from the training images.

nodes.label: Localisation & SLAM
nodes.summary: Estimate the robot's pose against a map, or build the map while localising (SLAM).
nodes.outcome: Explain why loop closure matters in SLAM.
nodes.check: What does loop closure do in SLAM?
nodes.answer: Recognising a previously visited place lets the robot correct the drift accumulated around the loop.

nodes.label: Path & Coverage Planning
nodes.summary: Shortest paths (A*) between points, and coverage paths that visit every row with minimal turning.
nodes.outcome: Plan a coverage path for a field and a detour around an obstacle.
nodes.check: Why do field robots plan boustrophedon (back-and-forth) paths?
nodes.answer: They cover every row with minimal overlap and few turns, matching how crops are planted.

nodes.label: Robot Software (ROS)
nodes.summary: Nodes, topics and messages; simulation before field testing.
nodes.outcome: Wire sensor, planner and controller nodes over ROS topics.
nodes.check: Why test robot software in simulation before the field?
nodes.answer: It is cheaper, faster and safer to find bugs, and conditions can be repeated exactly.

nodes.label: Field Robotics in Agriculture
nodes.summary: Weeding, harvesting, spraying and phenotyping robots: soft handling of plants, all-weather operation, and economics against labour cost.
nodes.outcome: Specify a weeding robot: sensing, actuation, speed and payback.
nodes.check: Why is robotic fruit picking much harder than robotic weeding?
nodes.answer: Fruit is hidden by leaves, varies in shape and ripeness, and must be grasped gently without bruising.

nodes.label: Precision Agriculture
nodes.summary: Variable-rate application from yield maps, soil sensors and imagery: inputs placed only where they pay.
nodes.outcome: Build a variable-rate fertiliser map from yield and soil data.
nodes.check: What is the benefit of variable-rate fertiliser application over a uniform rate?
nodes.answer: Less fertiliser wasted and less runoff, because each zone gets what it needs.

nodes.label: Safety & Autonomy Levels
nodes.summary: Risk assessment, emergency stops, geofences and human detection for robots working near people and animals.
nodes.outcome: Write a risk assessment for an autonomous tractor.
nodes.check: Name two safety layers an autonomous tractor should have.
nodes.answer: E.g. an emergency stop (remote and on-board), obstacle/person detection, a geofence and a watchdog that stops on lost communication.
